demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
become overly compliant when feeling threatened
Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle

Threat.value: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't rely on other people
I can no longer trust my own body
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: 'Talks or photos about snakes' is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another unless the accident specifically involved a snake, which is not suggested anywhere else in the profile. The other trigger items point to generic post-traumatic cueing, but this item implies a highly specific trauma cue that lacks support from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' does not fit well with the trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another and is not supported by the other nodes. The profile otherwise centers on guilt, danger scanning, intrusive recollection, and distrust of self/body; betrayal by another person introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme without corroboration.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Avoiding emotional closeness/intimacy is weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The dominant threat and memory items concern danger, hypervigilance, intrusive imagery, numbness, and grief after an accidental injury event. Intimacy avoidance could occur, but here it appears to address an interpersonal/betrayal theme that is not otherwise coherently represented, especially given the unsupported betrayal appraisal.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is dominated by generalized interpersonal/environmental danger monitoring (avoiding unfamiliar places, scanning exits in any room), which fits assault or deliberate threat contexts better than accidentally causing serious injury to another in an accident. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly focused on accidents, loss of control, or harm recurrence rather than pervasive escape-oriented vigilance across all settings.

issues.item: Threat: Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'I can't rely on other people' is weakly grounded in the rest of the profile. The other nodes center on accident-related triggers, guilt, bodily unreliability, and generalized hypervigilance, but there is no corresponding interpersonal betrayal, abandonment, or dependence theme to support this item. It stands out as clinically disconnected from the trauma narrative and the rest of the selected items.

vignette: On a bright spring afternoon, 19‑year‑old Anika, a hairdresser in a bustling downtown salon, was hurrying home after a long shift when a delivery truck lost its lane and veered into the crosswalk. She was the only one on the sidewalk, and the truck’s brakes failed to stop in time. The collision sent a concrete slab tumbling onto the road, shattering glass, and in a split second the world became a blur of headlights and screeching metal. The accident left a woman seriously injured, and Anika felt the crushing weight of guilt that she had somehow caused it. Even months later, the memory of that instant lingers as a vivid, sharp image in her mind, each replay punctuated by the thud of tires and the shriek of broken glass. The memory is accompanied by intrusive thoughts of the scene, a sudden rush of loud noises—her own racing heart and the blaring horns—and a mental replay of cars colliding with such ferocity. These triggers—intrusive thoughts, crash imagery, and loud noises—reawaken the day after the event, when she hears traffic or hears a sudden clatter. In those moments Anika finds herself unable to relax even when she knows she is in a safe environment, and she scans every room for exits, feeling as though danger could burst from any corner. The very triggers that summon the memory also awaken a sense of threat, causing her body to react strongly whenever she encounters something that reminds her of the accident. The vividness of the images, coupled with her inability to calm herself, fuels a belief that she cannot rely on others or on her own body; she feels the body has betrayed her by allowing her to be in a situation that could have been avoided. She also harbors the painful conviction that she failed to protect the injured woman, a thought that deepens her sense of failure. These negative appraisals feed back into her experience of the event, reinforcing the memory of the collision as a powerful, shame‑laden episode that she cannot escape. The triggers, the threat, and the negative appraisals together push her toward maladaptive strategies. She avoids the date of the accident, refusing to celebrate any anniversary that might remind her of the day. She also begins to fawn over clients and colleagues, becoming overly compliant and eager to placate anyone who might appear threatening. The fear of another crash or of being caught again in a dangerous situation leads her to avoid driving altogether; she refuses to drive, and she even resists being a passenger in a vehicle. These behaviors, while intended to keep her safe, become part of her daily routine, coloring her interactions at work and at home. As the months went on, the negative appraisals that had begun after the crash became entrenched. The belief that she could not rely on others and that her own body was unreliable made her retreat further into herself, reinforcing her feeling that the world was hostile. When she thought of the injured woman, the image of her lying on the asphalt, the thought that she had failed to protect her, she would see flashes of the crash, bringing back the same intrusive thoughts and loud noises. The memory, in turn, kept those negative appraisals vivid, as if the trauma were still unfolding. The sense of threat—unable to relax, constantly scanning for exits, and experiencing strong physical reactions—was now the backdrop to each day. The threat spurred her to continue avoiding driving and to become more compliant, as if compliance could neutralize a potential threat. Yet, each time she avoided driving or complied with others, the memory seemed to surface anew, reinforced by the fact that she was staying away from what she thought might be dangerous. The threat also made the triggers more potent, because the knowledge that she could be hurt again made the loud noises and crash imagery more jarring. All of these interactions kept the negative appraisals, triggers, and threat alive in a self‑reinforcing loop that seeped into every aspect of her life. Her maladaptive strategies—avoiding anniversaries, fawning over others, and shunning driving—became the visible face of her internal conflict. Each avoidance action triggered new memories of the crash, as she could not help but remember the sound of brakes squealing or the sight of a broken street. The strategies also fed back into her negative appraisals: every time she avoided a familiar day or became overly compliant, she felt more isolated, more unable to rely on others, and more certain that her body had failed her. The strategies themselves increased her sense of threat; the constant vigilance required to avoid driving kept her body in a state of hyper‑alertness, and the avoidance of anniversaries made her feel that the world could never be normal again. Finally, these strategies perpetuated the triggers: each time she avoided driving, she imagined the scene of the collision replaying in her mind, each image stoking the same intrusive thoughts and crash imagery she already feared. Now, at nineteen, Anika sits in the quiet of her apartment after closing the salon, her fingers hovering over the phone that she has been reluctant to answer for weeks. The thought of stepping outside, of hearing traffic, of hearing a sudden clatter, overwhelms her. Yet the fear of staying isolated, of feeling numb and helpless, is even greater. She has finally decided to seek help, because she can no longer tolerate the relentless cycle of thoughts that haunt her. She fears that if she does not change her patterns, her job and her relationship will unravel; she hopes that a therapist can help her find a way to trust herself and others again, to move beyond the images that no longer belong to her life.
